(1) We have developed a fast algorithm, ZHS-thinned, for simulating electromagnetic cascades in dense media.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a new code, ZHS-thinned, for the simulation of electromagnetic cascades in dense media at ultra-high energies.

the development and application of numerical methods for the simulation of electromagnetic cascades in dense media, in particular the simulation of the coherent radio emission produced by such cascades.

the development of fast, accurate simulation techniques for electromagnetic cascades, and the associated coherent radiation, in dense media, with a particular application to radio detection of high-energy neutrinos.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ZHS-thinned code, with the new parameterisations, provides a fast, accurate and flexible tool for simulating the radio signal produced by high-energy showers in dense media.
the new parameterizations presented in this paper are a significant improvement on the previous ones.
the ZHS-thinned code is a fast and reliable tool for the simulation of the electromagnetic cascades and coherent radio signals produced by neutrino interactions in ice, salt and regolith.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a fast and accurate method to simulate the electromagnetic showers induced by neutrino interactions in ice, salt and lunar regolith, including the LPM effect, and the coherent Cherenkov emission from such showers.

we are now able to simulate radio signals for neutrino interactions up to 10^20 eV, and we have developed parameterisations for the lunar regolith which should be useful for the detection of neutrinos from the lunar surface.

we can now simulate radio signals from neutrino showers at the highest energies, and we have developed parameterisations that allow us to simulate showers up to the maximum energies of the cosmic-ray spectrum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for a neutrino energy of E ν = 10 17 eV, and a target density of 0.8 g/cm 3, the radio detection probability is 10 − 5 for a target volume of 100 km 3.
, for a neutrino energy E ν = 10 17 eV and a target depth of 100 m, the radio detection probability is 10 3 times greater in salt than in water.
the radio technique can detect neutrinos of energies up to 10 EeV ( 10 20  eV ) at a depth of 1 km in ice, salt or the regolith.
